## The idea

Remove the short notes between a melody's longer arrivals and a plain harmonic
skeleton often appears. Restore them and the line regains momentum, delay, and
small detours. Some restored pitches may not belong to the harmony sounding at
that instant, yet their paths into and out of stable tones make them intelligible.

A *passing tone* fills a step between two chord tones. A *neighbour tone* leaves
a chord tone by step and returns. A *suspension* carries a tone from the previous
harmony into the next before resolving downward. An *anticipation* reaches a
tone of the coming chord before that chord arrives. Each term describes behaviour
across time; an isolated pitch class cannot tell you which role it is playing.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 88
use_synth :piano

define :play_phrase do |events|
  events.each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.82
    sleep duration
  end
end

skeleton = [[:c4, 2], [:e4, 2], [:g4, 2], [:c5, 2]]

passing = [[:c4, 1], [:d4, 1], [:e4, 2],
           [:g4, 1], [:a4, 1], [:c5, 2]]

neighbor = [[:c4, 1], [:d4, 0.5], [:c4, 0.5], [:e4, 2],
            [:g4, 1], [:f4, 0.5], [:g4, 0.5], [:c5, 2]]

decorated = [[:c4, 1], [:d4, 1], [:e4, 1], [:f4, 1],
             [:g4, 1], [:a4, 0.5], [:b4, 0.5], [:c5, 2]]

[skeleton, passing, neighbor, decorated].each do |events|
  play_phrase events
  sleep 1
end
```

The skeleton presents four long targets with little motion between them. In the
array named `passing`, D fills the step from C to E; the later A introduces motion
between G and C without completing every intervening step. Neighbours circle
briefly away from a target and back. The most decorated line becomes
denser as it approaches the final C, giving a directional shape to the same
underlying harmonic outline.

## Change one thing

1. Change D in the passing line to D-sharp. It still occupies the register
   between C and E, but the route now consists of unequal semitone motions.
   Listen for the new emphasis created by the chromatic approach to E.
2. The program above contains no harmony timeline, so add one before testing a
   suspension: hold F major for two beats, move to C major for two, sustain F
   across that boundary, then resolve it down to E. F begins as a chord tone and
   becomes dissonant only when the harmony changes.
3. Use the same explicit timeline for an anticipation. Move the final C half a
   beat before the C-major chord arrives. The early note becomes stable when the
   harmony catches up; without the chord boundary, the label would be unsupported.

## Why it works

Chord membership must be evaluated at a particular time. C is stable over C
major, may decorate another harmony, and can anticipate a coming A-minor chord.
To classify the melodic event, a program needs the harmony aligned with its
onset and duration. The note value alone is insufficient.

Reduction chooses notes that appear structurally stable, often because of their
metric position, duration, or harmonic membership. Decoration then explains the
routes between those points. The process is interpretive and loses information.
When rhythm or harmony is ambiguous, two plausible reductions may preserve
different skeletons. Playing both makes that analytical disagreement audible.

The example arrays keep pitch beside duration. A richer event record could add
`:role`, but playback would still consume the original note and timing. The
role belongs to the analytical description rather than to the physical act of
rendering a pitch. Keeping those concerns apart allows an interpretation to
change without silently rewriting the source melody.

Metric position changes the likely reading. A dissonant step on a weak half-beat
can pass almost unnoticed. Sustain the same pitch across a strong beat and it
asks for a stronger explanation, perhaps as a suspension. Duration, preparation,
and destination contribute too. Set membership can flag a non-chord tone, but
it cannot name the behaviour without examining neighbouring events in time.

Reduction also provides a way to compose. Begin with stable destinations and
decide whether each gap needs direct motion, delay, or a brief departure and
return. Add one decoration, then replay the phrase. If every opening receives an
ornament, the destinations can lose their hierarchy. The program's alternating
versions keep that trade-off available to the ear.

## Take it further

Write a two-bar melody over C major followed by G major. Include one passing
tone, neighbour, suspension, and anticipation, and label each role in an event
hash containing `:note`, `:start`, `:duration`, and `:role`. The renderer should
ignore the analytical field. Then print and play a reduction containing only
`:chord_tone` events. Compare the plain destinations with the full line and
check that every decoration can be explained by its preparation and destination.
